summary: Discusses how L2TP can use IPsec to provide tunnel authentication, privacy, integrity checking, and replay protection, covering both voluntary and compulsory tunneling.

plainLanguage.summary: L2TP carries a dial-up or point-to-point connection across a network by wrapping each frame in a tunnel. This RFC says how to put IPsec underneath that tunnel, so the frames and the tunnel setup messages are authenticated, checked for tampering, protected against replay, and optionally encrypted. It also works through the awkward case where the tunnel's port number or address changes while it is being set up.

subtitle: How to protect L2TP tunnels with IPsec ESP and IKE, including the filter rules when ports and addresses move.

tldr.problem: L2TP tunnels PPP traffic across a network but defines no way to protect the tunnel itself, so the control and data packets are open to snooping, modification, hijacking and denial of service.
tldr.mechanism: L2TP is protected by running IPsec ESP underneath it, with IKE to agree the keys and the filter rules that bind each security association to a particular tunnel, including when the tunnel's port numbers or addresses change during setup.
tldr.outcome: The document sets out the security services L2TP must provide, the IPsec configuration that meets them, and the per-packet checks L2TP must make, and it explains the gap that remains: IPsec authenticates the machine, not the user.

today:
RFC 3193 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the document that describes how to protect L2TP with IPsec.

The memo does not claim that L2TP over IPsec is a complete answer. It says plainly that it does not attempt to standardize end-to-end security, and it records the gap that remains: with machine authentication, once the tunnel is open any user on that machine can typically send traffic down it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
L2TP is a protocol that tunnels PPP traffic over a variety of networks such as IP, SONET and ATM. Because the protocol encapsulates PPP, L2TP inherits PPP authentication as well as the PPP Encryption Control Protocol and the PPP Compression Control Protocol. L2TP also includes support for tunnel authentication, which can be used to mutually authenticate the tunnel endpoints. It does not, however, define tunnel protection mechanisms.

IPsec is a protocol suite used to secure communication at the network layer between two peers. It is made up of the IP Security Architecture document, IKE for key management, and the Authentication Header and Encapsulating Security Payload for protecting IP traffic.

This document proposes the use of the IPsec protocol suite for protecting L2TP traffic over IP networks, and discusses how IPsec and L2TP should be used together. It does not attempt to standardize end-to-end security: when end-to-end security is required, the recommendation is to use additional security mechanisms such as IPsec or TLS inside the tunnel, in addition to L2TP tunnel security. Although L2TP does not mandate IP and UDP for its transport, the scope of the document is limited to L2TP over IP networks, and the mechanisms for enabling security over non-IP networks must be addressed in the standards for L2TP over those networks.
sections.plainLanguage: L2TP wraps a point-to-point link inside a tunnel so it can cross an ordinary IP network. It has no encryption of its own, so this RFC puts IPsec under it. The scope is narrow: it protects the tunnel between the two ends, not the traffic that travels inside the tunnel from the client to the final server.

sections.title: L2TP Security Requirements
sections.content:
L2TP tunnels PPP traffic over IP and non-IP public networks, so both the control and the data packets of the L2TP protocol are vulnerable to attack. The document lists the attacks. An adversary may try to discover user identities by snooping data packets, or to modify packets, whether control or data. An adversary may try to hijack the L2TP tunnel or the PPP connection inside the tunnel. An adversary can launch denial of service attacks by terminating PPP connections or L2TP tunnels. And an adversary may attempt to disrupt the PPP Encryption Control Protocol negotiation in order to weaken or remove confidentiality protection, or disrupt the PPP Link Control Protocol authentication negotiation so as to weaken the PPP authentication process or gain access to user passwords.

To address these threats, the L2TP security protocol must provide authentication, integrity and replay protection for control packets, and should be able to protect their confidentiality. It must provide integrity and replay protection for data packets, and may protect their confidentiality. It must also provide a scalable approach to key management.

The document explains why the mechanisms L2TP already has are not enough. L2TP tunnel authentication provides mutual authentication between the LAC and the LNS at tunnel origination, so it does not protect control and data traffic on a per-packet basis, and the tunnel stays vulnerable. PPP authenticates the client to the LNS but provides no per-packet authentication, integrity or replay protection. PPP encryption meets the confidentiality requirement for PPP traffic but does not address authentication, integrity, replay protection or key management, and the PPP Encryption Control Protocol negotiation does not provide a protected ciphersuite negotiation, so PPP encryption is a weak security solution and does nothing for the L2TP control channel.
sections.plainLanguage: The document lists what can go wrong: someone reading the traffic to learn who is calling, changing packets, taking over the tunnel, cutting the connection, or interfering with the negotiation that would otherwise encrypt the inner PPP connection. The existing pieces do not close these holes, because the checks happen once at setup rather than on every packet.

sections.title: The L2TP Security Protocol
sections.content:
All L2TP security compliant implementations must implement IPsec ESP for securing both L2TP control and data packets. Transport mode must be supported, and tunnel mode may be supported. All the IPsec-mandated ciphersuites, including NULL encryption, must be supported, although it is an operator choice which of them are actually used. If confidentiality is not required, for example for L2TP data traffic, ESP with NULL encryption may be used. The implementations must implement the replay protection mechanisms of IPsec.

L2TP security must meet the key management requirements of the IPsec protocol suite. IKE should be supported for authentication, security association negotiation and key management, using the IPsec DOI.
sections.plainLanguage: The protection is IPsec's ESP, in transport mode, and it applies to the tunnel setup messages as well as to the traffic inside the tunnel. The keys come from IKE. An implementation has to offer every cipher IPsec requires, even though the operator picks which one is actually used, and it may use ESP without encryption where only an integrity check is wanted.

sections.title: Interoperability Guidelines
sections.content:
When an L2TP tunnel is torn down, whether gracefully or not, the control connection teardown mechanism defined in the L2TP specification must be used. Once the tunnel has been deleted by either peer, any phase 1 and phase 2 security associations that still exist as a result of the tunnel between the peers should be deleted, and phase 1 and phase 2 delete messages should be sent. When IKE receives such a delete message it should notify L2TP, and a Zero Length Body acknowledgement sent in response to a StopCCN can be taken as positive acknowledgement that the peer received it and has torn down its L2TP state, after which the tunnel state and its filters can be removed.

Because the default MRU for PPP connections is 1500 bytes, fragmentation becomes a concern when the L2TP and IPsec headers are prepended to a PPP frame. One way to reduce the problem is to give PPP the MTU value of the ingress or egress interface of the L2TP and IPsec tunnel, minus the overhead of the extra headers. This should happen after the L2TP tunnel has been set up but before the LCP negotiations begin, and if the tunnel interface has a smaller MTU than PPP's default it may replace the value in use. That value may also be proposed as the initial MRU in the LCP Configure-Request. If an ICMP packet too big message is received by IPsec, the value should be stored in the security association, and IPsec should notify L2TP so the new MTU can be reflected into the PPP interface; new path MTU discoveries at the PPP interface should then be checked against the new value.

When a packet arrives from a tunnel that requires security, L2TP must first check that the packet was decrypted or authenticated by IPsec. Since IPsec verifies that the packet arrived in the correct security association, L2TP can be assured that it was sent by a trusted peer and did not arrive in the clear. L2TP must then verify that the IP addresses and UDP port values in the packet match the socket information that was used to set the L2TP tunnel up, which prevents a malicious peer from spoofing packets into other tunnels.
sections.plainLanguage: Three practical points. When the tunnel closes, the IPsec protections it held should be torn down with it, or they linger. The extra headers take space, so PPP should be told a smaller maximum packet size than its default. And on every arriving packet, L2TP checks two things: that IPsec already accepted the packet, and that the addresses and ports in it are the ones this tunnel was set up with, so a peer cannot slip a packet into somebody else's tunnel.

sections.title: IPsec Filtering Details
sections.content:
IKE and IPsec are agnostic about the nuances of the application they protect, so normally no integration is needed. Protocols that let the port number float during negotiation, L2TP among them, can cause problems within the current IKE framework, because the L2TP specification allows an implementation to use a dynamically assigned UDP source port, and the port change is reflected in the SCCRP sent from the responder to the initiator.

The document therefore works through the eight combinations of a fixed or dynamic initiator port, a fixed or dynamic responder address, and a fixed or dynamic responder port. Solving the most general case covers all of them: the initiator chooses a new port number and the responder chooses both a new address and a new port number.

The general case runs as follows. IKE phase 1 and phase 2 protect the initial SCCRQ, which is sent from a fixed IP address with a dynamic initiator port. The responder replies with a StopCCN because it has chosen a new IP address, and the address is carried in the error message of the Result and Error Code AVP, with the Result Code set to 2 for a general error and the Error Code set to 7 for try another. A new IKE phase 1 and phase 2 then protect a new SCCRQ, sent to the responder's new IP address, and a further IKE phase 2 handles the responder's port number change. The responder then sends the SCCRP with its new port number, and the initiator replies with the SCCCN, completing the tunnel.

To support the general case, mechanisms have to be designed into L2TP and IPsec that allow L2TP to inject filters into the IPsec filter database. The document defines the filter sets for the initiator and the responder at each stage, using the terms I-Port and R-Port for the UDP port numbers the two ends chose, R-IPAddr1 for the address the responder listens on for the initial SCCRQ, R-IPAddr2 for the address it chooses after receiving it, R-IPAddr for whichever of the two is in use, and I-IPAddr for the initiator's address. Two special values appear: Any-Addr, which tells IKE to accept any single address proposed by the peer, and Any-Port, which tells IKE to accept a value of 0 or a specific port value.

The filters are listed from highest priority to lowest. Before the tunnel setup messages flow, the initial filter set must be in place, either pre-configured on both ends or injected by L2TP. The responder's inbound filter accepts from any address to R-IPAddr1, UDP, source any port, destination 1701. The initiator's outbound filter sends from I-IPAddr to R-IPAddr1, UDP, source I-Port, destination 1701, and its two inbound filters accept from R-IPAddr1 to I-IPAddr, UDP, source 1701 or any port, destination I-Port. The Any-Port in the second inbound filter is what handles a port change by the responder. If the initiator uses a dynamic port, L2TP must inject these filters once the source port is known; if it uses the fixed port 1701 they may be static.

In the gateway-to-gateway and L2TP dial-out cases, where either side may initiate, the initial filter set at both ends must additionally include an inbound filter from any address to R-IPAddr1, UDP, source any port, destination 1701.
sections.plainLanguage: The hard part is that L2TP is allowed to change its port number, and even its address, while the tunnel is being set up, and IPsec's rules are written in terms of fixed addresses and ports. The document's answer is a set of filter rules that both ends install in the IPsec filter database, in a defined order, as the setup proceeds, and a StopCCN message that carries the new address as plain text.

sections.title: Authentication Issues
sections.content:
IPsec IKE negotiation must negotiate an authentication method specified in the IKE RFC. In addition to IKE authentication, L2TP implementations use PPP authentication methods.

The document draws a careful distinction. PPP provides initial authentication but no per-packet authentication, integrity or replay protection, so the identity verified during the initial PPP authentication is not verified again when each packet arrives. With IPsec, once the identity asserted in IKE is authenticated, the derived keys provide per-packet authentication, integrity and replay protection, so the identity verified in the IKE conversation is verified on every packet.

Assume the identity claimed in PPP is a user identity and the identity claimed within IKE is a machine identity. Because only the machine identity is verified per packet, there is no way to verify that only the user who authenticated within PPP is using the tunnel. An IPsec implementation that supports only machine authentication typically has no way to enforce traffic segregation, so where machine authentication is used, once an L2TP and IPsec tunnel is open, any user on a multi-user machine will typically be able to send traffic down it. If the IPsec implementation supports user authentication the problem can be averted, because the user identity asserted within IKE is then verified per packet, and the client must then ensure that only traffic from that particular user is sent down the tunnel.

When X.509 certificate authentication is chosen within IKE, the LNS is expected to use an IKE Certificate Request Payload to ask the client for a certificate issued by a particular authority, or several such payloads if several authorities are trusted and configured in its authentication policy. The LNS should be able to trust several certificate authorities, so that tunnel clients can connect with their own certificate credentials from their own PKI, and client and server side certificate revocation list checking may be enabled on a per-authority basis. L2TP implementations may use dynamically assigned ports for both source and destination only if security for each source and destination port combination can be successfully negotiated by IKE.

The certificate credentials the client provides may be those of the machine or of the L2TP user. Because the value of a machine certificate is inversely proportional to the ease with which an attacker can obtain one under false pretenses, the machine certificate enrolment process should be strictly controlled, so that only administrators can enrol a machine with a machine certificate. Smartcard storage lessens the chance of the private key being compromised, though smartcards are not necessarily desirable in all situations, and moving a machine certificate from one machine to another may be undesirable where the dual assurance of machine and user authentication is valued. Where user certificates are deployed, the user enrolment process should likewise be strictly controlled: if a user password can readily be used to obtain a certificate, that certificate has no more security value than the password, so the enrolment period can be limited, after which password access is turned off.

Pre-shared keys in IKE main mode are vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks in remote access situations. In main mode it is necessary for SKEYID_e to be used before the identification payload is received, so the selection of the pre-shared key may only be based on information in the IP header. In remote access, dynamic IP address assignment is typical, so it is often not possible to identify the required key by address. The same pre-shared key is then shared by a group of users and no longer functions as an effective shared secret, and neither the client nor the server identifies itself during IKE phase 1; this permits anyone with access to the group key to act as a man-in-the-middle. The vulnerability does not occur in aggressive mode, because the identity payload is sent earlier in the exchange and the key can be selected on the basis of that identity, but aggressive mode exposes the user identity, which is often considered undesirable. As a result, where main mode is used with pre-shared keys and PPP does not perform mutual authentication, the server is not authenticated, which enables a rogue server holding the group key to masquerade as the LNS and mount a dictionary attack on legacy authentication methods such as CHAP, potentially compromising many passwords at once. L2TP and IPsec implementations should therefore not use a group pre-shared key for IKE authentication to the LNS, and the pre-shared key values should be protected in a manner similar to the user's account password used by L2TP.
sections.plainLanguage: The key point is what each layer proves. PPP proves who the user is once, at the start. IPsec proves which machine is on the other end on every packet. So a tunnel protected by machine certificates lets any user of that machine use the tunnel, unless the client is careful to send only one user's traffic down it. The document also warns against a group password used for IKE, because in that case neither end proves who it is.

sections.title: IPsec and PPP Security Interactions
sections.content:
When L2TP is protected with IPsec, both PPP and IPsec security services are available, and which are negotiated depends on whether the tunnel is compulsory or voluntary. The document notes that these scenarios are non-normative and create no requirements for an implementation to be L2TP security compliant.

In the compulsory tunnel case the client sends PPP frames to the LAC and will typically not be aware that the frames are being tunnelled, or that any security services are in place between the LAC and the LNS. At the LNS a data packet arrives that includes a PPP frame encapsulated in L2TP, itself encapsulated in an IP packet. By reading the properties of the security association set up between the LNS and the LAC, the LNS can learn what security services are in place between itself and the LAC, so in the compulsory case the client and the LNS have unequal knowledge of the security services in place between them.

Because the LNS knows whether confidentiality, authentication, integrity and replay protection are in place, it can change its behaviour during the PPP ECP and CCP negotiations. If the LNS policy is require encryption, allow encryption or prohibit encryption, then with IPsec confidentiality in place an LNS with a prohibit encryption policy acts as though the policy had been violated, while an LNS with a require or allow policy acts as though the policy had been satisfied and would not mandate the use of PPP encryption or compression. That is not the same as insisting that PPP encryption and compression be turned off, since the decision depends on client policy.

Since the client has no knowledge of the security services in place between the LAC and the LNS, and may not trust the LAC or the wire between itself and the LAC, the client will typically want to ensure sufficient security by using end-to-end IPsec or PPP encryption and compression between itself and the LNS. A client that wants security over the entire path will negotiate confidentiality between itself and the LNS to get privacy on the wire to the LAC, and negotiate end-to-end security between itself and the end station for the part of the path from the LNS onwards. The client will typically not trust the LAC and will negotiate confidentiality and compression itself, so the LAC may wish to negotiate only IPsec ESP with null encryption towards the LNS, with the LNS requesting replay protection. That avoids duplicating confidentiality and compression over the path from the LAC to the LNS and scales better, because encryption is handled by the client and the LNS.

In the voluntary tunnel case the client sends L2TP packets to the NAS, which routes them to the LNS, and over a dial-up link those packets are encapsulated in IP and PPP. If the client can retrieve the properties of the security association between itself and the LNS, it knows the security services negotiated, as well as the PPP encryption and compression services negotiated with the NAS. From the LNS point of view the situation is identical to the compulsory case, but because the client also knows the services in place, the client and the LNS have symmetric knowledge. The LNS can behave as though a require encryption directive had been fulfilled, and typically will not insist that PPP encryption or compression be turned off, leaving that decision to the client. The client, knowing IPsec ESP is already in place, can request that PPP encryption and compression not be negotiated, and if IP compression services cannot be negotiated it is typically desirable to turn off PPP compression when no stateless method is available, because of the undesirable effects of stateful PPP compression. The two can therefore typically avoid PPP encryption and compression altogether. This may result in duplicate encryption when the client talks to an IPsec-capable end station, which the client may avoid by negotiating two security associations with the LNS, one with ESP with null encryption and one with confidentiality and compression, routing packets to an IPsec-capable end station over the first. Many IPsec implementations cannot support this without allowing L2TP packets on the same tunnel to be originated from multiple UDP ports, which requires modifications to the L2TP specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Whether the client knows the tunnel is protected changes what the two ends negotiate. In a compulsory tunnel the client is not told, so it protects itself and the server must not turn on PPP encryption as well or the data is encrypted twice. In a voluntary tunnel both ends know, so they can usually switch PPP encryption off and rely on IPsec alone.
